title: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce
description: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday i
body: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams. "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. "Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said. Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20. The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want."Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier.Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance. The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership.And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month, Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees, with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles.— CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce

title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 41% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
description: Matteo Danieli, co-founder of Bending Spoons, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on
body: Matteo Danieli, co-founder of Bending Spoons, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Wednesday, July 1, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesShares of Bending Spoons skyrocketed 41% after a new securities filing revealed that Berkshire Hathaway made a fresh $330 million investment into the company.The latest infusion follows the conglomerate's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq.Under the deal, Bending Spoons will issue 10 million ordinary shares to Berkshire at $33 a share. "Bending Spoons continuously evaluates M&A opportunities, and our pipeline remains strong," said Francesco Patarnello, Bending Spoons' co-founder and head of business acquisitions, in a statement. "We believe Berkshire Hathaway's investment reflects confidence in our team and Platform and will further enhance our financial flexibility and ability to pursue attractive acquisitions as part of our broader financing strategy."The investment now brings Berkshire's stake in the company to 4%, according to the filing, and is the conglomerate's latest investment decision as CEO Greg Abel took the helm from founder and legendary investor Warren Buffett at the start of the year. title: Jim Cramer says don't give up on this unpredictable market. Here's why
description: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Wed, Oct 14 20266:19 PM EDTKey PointsDespite an unpredictable market, CNBC's Jim Cramer says its
body: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Wed, Oct 14 20266:19 PM EDTKey PointsDespite an unpredictable market, CNBC's Jim Cramer says its important to stay invested. "You just want to throw things away and go home," the "Mad Money" host said. "If you do, though, will you be able to buy them back in time for those ten days of the year where all the gains are made? I don't think so."While strong earnings were not enough to rescue stocks in this unpredictable market, CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Wednesday that investors who give up now could miss out on the next rally.Stocks tumbled on the session, with the S&P 500 down just over 1%, the Nasdaq shedding 1.9% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing slightly lower.Cramer said that uncertainty surrounding inflation, interest rates and the war with Iran makes it nearly impossible to anticipate the market's next move. "You just want to throw things away and go home," the "Mad Money" host added. "If you do, though, will you be able to buy them back in time for those 10 days of the year where all the gains are made? I don't think so." Historical market data underscores that risk. According to JPMorgan, an investor who put $10,000 into the S&P 500 and missed its 10 best trading days between 2005 and 2024 would have ended up with less than half the wealth of someone who stayed fully invested.  Cramer pointed to Wednesday's inflation report as an example of the market's unpredictability. Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September from the previous month, slightly more than expected, initially sending Treasury yields higher. They later reversed course, even as oil prices continued climbing. Typically, hotter inflation pushes yields higher as investors anticipate more aggressive interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve. The conflicting signals have complicated the expectations game regarding the Federal Reserve's next move. Another rate hike could slow the economy, while holding rates steady risks pushing long-term borrowing costs higher. Cramer argued that an end to the war with Iran could send oil prices sharply lower, easing inflation without further Fed intervention. Corporate earnings have offered little clarity. Investment bank Morgan Stanley reported a decent quarter, but shares still fell nearly 3%. Similarly, semiconductor equipment maker ASML reported strong earnings and growing demand, only to see its stock reverse early gains and close down 4% alongside the broader chip sector rout.With economic data and corporate results failing to provide clear direction, he said that "it becomes very hard to have conviction." Still, he cautioned against abandoning stocks altogether. Even investors who successfully avoid further losses risk missing the market's eventual recovery.

schema.headline: Jim Cramer says don't give up on this unpredictable market. Here's why

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
description: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligen
body: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker."We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

title: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million
description: watch nowMorgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the
body: watch nowMorgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the company reported:Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimateRevenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion LSEG estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue rose 12% to $20.34 billion.The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million.Morgan Stanley noted widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere.Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower initial public offerings and a drop in fixed income underwriting.Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. Morgan Stanley shares declined about 3% Wednesday.The economy is subject to two key forces right now: the boost from the artificial intelligence build-out and the drag from geopolitical strife, Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick told CNBC's Leslie Picker on Wednesday.Starting in early September, concerns with overseas conflict, inflation and surging yields slowed activity across Wall Street, Pick noted."The interaction of the AI phenomenon and geopolitics has been the dominant reality the whole year," Pick said. "It's really two very different stories, and I'd like to think that we are going to have the first narrative, the positive narrative, if we can get some control over the geopolitics."Pick is "cautiously optimistic" about markets in the fourth quarter, he added.

schema.headline: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million

title: 10-year Treasury yield dips as traders look ahead to Thursday economic reports
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on September 16, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty Im
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on September 16, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesThe 10-year Treasury note yield fell on Wednesday after jumping earlier in the day as traders awaited more inflation data due out Thursday.The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 2 basis points to 5.19%. Earlier in the day, yields had climbed in reaction to a stronger-than-expected September consumer price index report. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury yield — which tends to react most to geopolitical events — was down more than 4 basis points at 5.517%. The 2-year Treasury yield — which closely tracks the Fed's interest rate decisions — gained more than 1 basis point to 4.808% after earlier hitting its highest level since Sept. 29.One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely.The midday reversal came as equities sold off, with the S&P 500 dropping more than 1%, leading some investors to rotate back into the relative safety of the bond market.On Thursday, investors will get the September reading for the producer price index, September retail sales data and weekly initial jobless claims figures. For PPI, economists polled by Dow Jones are expecting a 0.6% rise on the month and a 5.5% gain on the year.The data will follow Wednesday's September consumer price index report, which rose 3.7% year over year, higher than the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 3.6%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, came in at 2.6% on an annualized basis, versus the 2.5% consensus estimate. The latest inflation reading comes just two weeks before the Fed's next interest rate decision. With inflation remaining sticky, the central bank may need to raise rates higher and keep them there for longer in 2027, said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds."The bond bulls have turned around and are running the other way as 10-year yields have shot higher after today's shocking inflation report," he said. "Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates."Odds for an October 28 quarter-point hike in the fed funds rate — currently 3.75% to 4.00% — increased to roughly 35% from just 22.1% a day ago, according to futures trading measured by CME's FedWatch tool.There is now more than a 90% likelihood of at least one more rate hike before the year is out, and included in that is a 40% chance that rates are higher by a half-percentage point — double the odds seen just one day ago.— With additional reporting by CNBC's John Melloy.

title: Bank of America shares drop after third-quarter revenue miss and regulatory penalty
description: watch nowBank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also
body: watch nowBank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected.Shares of the bank fell almost 5% on Wednesday. Here's what the company reported:Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEGRevenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEGThe bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share.Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations.Fixed income trading revenue dropped 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate.Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million.The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%.Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance.Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate.'Worst in class'In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter.The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, sparked questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets.On the company's earnings call Wednesday, several analysts remarked on the sharp decline in Bank of America shares and pressed Moynihan about earlier guidance that compliance costs would be contained."Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning," JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja said. "It's not that you can't absorb a billion. … But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue."Other analysts questioned management on the pace of future share repurchases and asked about the bank's underperformance in trading. Management blamed the firm's bond trading results on the sharp rise in interest rates during the period."It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for" credit and mortgage trading businesses, CFO Alastair Borthwick said. 'The right course'Later Wednesday in an interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker, Moynihan didn't commit to a timeline on the resolution of regulatory issues. "We got to do the work, and then the regulators look at it," Moynihan said. "So I don't want to speculate about the precise timeline." The CEO added that he was "confident that we are on the right course to remediate everything."Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, added 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. Correction: Bank of America reported third-quarter revenue on an FTE basis of $30.12 billion compared with LSEG estimates of $30.69 billion. An earlier version misstated the comparison.

title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
description: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Uk
body: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply. Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22.However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making that tightening of supply feel that much more acute.Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.watch now

title: Jim Cramer explains why even strong bank earnings couldn't save their stocks
description: The nation's biggest banks delivered mixed third-quarter results this week, but Wall Street's reaction was overwhelmingly negative, with all six major
body: The nation's biggest banks delivered mixed third-quarter results this week, but Wall Street's reaction was overwhelmingly negative, with all six major bank stocks falling despite some strong results.CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday, on Day 2 of the financial earnings flood, that investors appear more concerned about what lies ahead than what the banks just reported."Frankly, it's strange to see such universally negative reactions to a set of quarters that contained plenty of positives," the "Mad Money" host said. "But this is what happens when investors are worried about the future, and it's hard not to worry with persistent inflation, rising interest rates, and newly wobbly capital markets."Here's what stood out from each bank's report.Wells FargoWells Fargo reported a mixed quarter Tuesday, beating earnings estimates but falling short on revenue. Net interest margin — a key profitability gauge, measuring the spread between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — stabilized at 2.43%, slightly ahead of expectations. That stabilization was particularly encouraging after the bank had missed net interest margin estimates in nine of the previous 10 quarters. Shares fell following the report, but Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio used by the CNBC Investing Club, upgraded the stock to a buy-equivalent rating. "CEO Charlie Scharf emphasized that his bank is set up to do much better in a higher interest rate environment and, given his track record, I believe him," Cramer said. Wells Fargo stock rose slightly Wednesday. JPMorgan Chase JPMorgan Chase missed expectations on both the top and bottom lines on Tuesday. Weakness in fixed income trading and asset management weighed on results, while expenses rose faster than revenue. On the earnings call, though, management offered better-than-expected net interest income forecasts for the fourth quarter and 2027. The stock initially struggled but recovered much of its losses as investors digested the outlook. For Cramer, the quarter "wasn't much of a needle-mover for the world's largest bank." JPMorgan stock gained nearly 1% in Wednesday's awful market.Citigroup Citigroup delivered one of the stronger headline reports on Tuesday. Revenue grew 8% year over year, marking the bank's best third-quarter performance in a decade, while management raised its full-year net interest income outlook. Citi also stood out as the only major bank to exceed fixed-income trading revenue expectations. Despite those positives, shares tumbled 5.6% following the report. "My suspicion is that Citi's stock was punished for its recent outperformance," Cramer said. "Before yesterday's beatdown, it was running circles around the rest of the group. But if you believe in the turnaround, as I do, this is a buying opportunity." Citi shares dropped another 1.8% on Wednesday.Bank of America On Wednesday, Bank of America delivered one of the most disappointing reports of the group, missing revenue and earnings expectations while also contending with a $1.2 billion regulatory penalty tied to alleged violations of anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws. The bank's capital markets businesses were particularly weak, with investment banking fees declining 11% and fixed-income trading revenue falling 17%. Although management highlighted continued growth in deposits and lending, those positives weren't enough to offset the disappointing results. Shares fell roughly 5% following the print.Goldman Sachs  Goldman Sachs "put up some excellent numbers" Tuesday, comfortably beating top and bottom line estimates. Investment banking fees rose 21%, while equities trading revenue surged 72%, offsetting weaker-than-expected fixed-income trading. Management also struck an optimistic tone, highlighting opportunities to finance the AI infrastructure buildout and a robust investment banking backlog. Yet shares surrendered an early rally and finished Tuesday slightly lower. "When a company reports such strong numbers and the stock gets slammed anyway, that tells you there are a lot of skeptics out there," he said. "They think the boom times are over. I don't agree, but that's the market's verdict, at least for the moment." Cramer's Charitable Trust upgraded Goldman to a buy-equivalent rating following the report, viewing the pullback as a buying opportunity. The stock lost another 1.5% on Wednesday.Morgan StanleyMorgan Stanley also topped expectations on Wednesday. The bank's Institutional Securities Group, which houses its investment banking and sales and trading segments, saw revenue rise 18%, while wealth management revenue grew 10%. CEO Ted Pick said that he was "cautiously optimistic about the fourth quarter," with the bank reportedly positioned to lead Anthropic's anticipated IPO. Still, shares fell almost 3% despite the solid results, reflecting investors' reluctance to reward even better-than-expected earnings amid broader concerns about the banking sector.

schema.headline: Jim Cramer explains why even strong bank earnings couldn't save their stocks

title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
description: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while
body: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while playing a key role in Operation Epic Fury and regional maritime security operations in the Middle East. Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesSaudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom. The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday.Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war.Iran 'counting the moments' until it can attack U.S. shipsIran Revolutionary Guard chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media. "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview. "We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens."CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.  Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile."In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control. "IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."Correction: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election. An earlier version misstated the day.

title: Delta's business-class revamp: New seats, menus, plates and more Porsches
description: Delta A350 fleet renderings with the next-generation Delta One suite cabin.Courtesy: DeltaDelta Air Lines, the country's most profitable airline, has
body: Delta A350 fleet renderings with the next-generation Delta One suite cabin.Courtesy: DeltaDelta Air Lines, the country's most profitable airline, has a problem serving its top-tier customers: not enough Porsches.The airline uses a fleet of 40 of the luxury vehicles to drive its high-value flyers right to the plane."What's happened over the last several years is the demand has continued to rise, and we realized that the 40 cars that we have weren't enough to meet the demand. So we're moving that fleet to 70," Ranjan Goswami, Delta's chief marketing and product officer, told CNBC.New Delta One meal service, including a recently designed saucier.Delta Air LinesIt's just one of many changes Delta is making for customers who fly in its most luxurious and expensive cabin, known as Delta One. The Porsche service is part of a VIP add-on option.The carrier on Wednesday unveiled new crockery for the cabins, new Missoni mini pillows and fresh food and beverage menus, including Champagne served over sorbet and Blanton's bourbon. Many of the new items will appear on flights originating in Los Angeles later this month and on other routes in the coming months.Delta is also planning to debut updated suites with a bigger screen and a more cushioned, lighter lie-flat seat when it starts flying its first Airbus A350-1000 planes early next year. Delta A350 fleet renderings with the next-generation Delta One suite cabin.Courtesy: DeltaDelta didn't announce changes to the coach and premium economy cabins.The airline's executives said the company is already thinking about adjustments on other aircraft, including smaller Airbus jets and on Boeing 787 Dreamliners that Delta has ordered and that will come in the next decade.watch nowDelta has invested heavily in premium service for close to two decades, and United Airlines has followed suit for a little over 10 years. Other carriers are also leaning into demand for higher-priced options.Read more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first class"You got to keep looking at the next cycle of what customers want, and you got to start planning for it now," Goswami said. He said Delta focused on details and quality with its latest project for Delta One so that the items, from sliding suite doors to new Delta-logo-emblazoned dinnerware, are made to last. The company tested some of those items to check for chipping, but there are other challenges, like customers liking them too much."I think people are going to love a couple of items, although we hope they don't steal them," he said.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

title: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
description: Bags of candy are displayed on a store's shelves on April 21, 2026, in Miami, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesU.S. consumers are in the midst of one
body: Bags of candy are displayed on a store's shelves on April 21, 2026, in Miami, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesU.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve.Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in."They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."Inflation by the numbersThe current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history. The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s.Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.How consumers respondOne of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy. Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth."Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.watch nowAt a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September, Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs."Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."Unhappy shoppersIn Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at a faster clip than wage growth in recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell to the lowest levels ever seen. The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in the grocery store produce aisle and when looking at airline flights for vacations.In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgone leisure activities like bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home."Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

schema.headline: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.

title: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico
description: US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.Samue
body: US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.Samuel Corum | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Department of Justice said Wednesday it is appealing a federal judge's decision to extend his order blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico.The notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit came less than a day after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the three outlets targeted by President Donald Trump can keep their access to the White House complex.That ruling, a preliminary injunction, replaces Kelly's temporary restraining order against the ban that Trump first announced on Sept. 18. It is not a final ruling in the ongoing lawsuit that the three news outlets filed against Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran and White House communications director Steven Cheung.Kelly, in an opinion filed Tuesday night, said the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claims that Trump and his co-defendants violated their First Amendment rights through unlawful retaliation and viewpoint discrimination."It is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," wrote Kelly, whom Trump nominated in 2017 for his current seat."In other words, it was 'an effort to suppress the speaker's activity due to disagreement with the speaker's view' ... rather than to vindicate any other purportedly 'compelling governmental interest,' ... including maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security," he wrote."Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote.Kelly was also unmoved by arguments that the decision to revoke the outlets' White House access was partly based on national security concerns "There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote.Trump did not mention national security in his initial Truth Social post announcing the ban, nor did he do so when asked about the move later that same day, Kelly noted."All this suggests that 'national security' was merely a post-hoc justification for the decision," the judge wrote.

schema.headline: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico

title: BlackRock's Larry Fink warns a data center moratorium could trigger a recession
description: watch nowBlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a halt to data center construction could trigger an economic slowdown."If we have a moratorium of some s
body: watch nowBlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a halt to data center construction could trigger an economic slowdown."If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession," Fink told CNBC Wednesday, after BlackRock reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings early Wednesday.  BlackRock advanced about 1% in late morning trading. "So much of our economy is based on the buildout of this capex," Fink added, referring to the massive investments made to develop artificial intelligence infrastructure.Fink's warning comes as strong, local opposition to data center construction has emerged as a key issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as communities struggle with rising utility costs, water use, environmental damage and questions over investment transparency.While Fink acknowledged fears about the data center buildout, he also noted "most of it is on misinformation." The stakes are high. Wall Street analysts estimate total AI capital expenditures could climb above $1 trillion in 2027 and total in excess of $5 trillion by 2030. "Data centers are not the problem. They're creating more new jobs than ever before," the BlackRock CEO explained. The scale of investment has created demand for construction workers, physical digital infrastructure, AI compute hardware and energy infrastructure to secure grid power, he said.

schema.headline: BlackRock's Larry Fink warns a data center moratorium could trigger a recession

title: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
description: watch nowCoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the
body: watch nowCoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 15.5%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves in a memo obtained by CNBC. "When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said. "The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back."Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes."Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk."'Relatively bad' balance sheetCoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained. "The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said. "It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave, 1 monthHe expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November.CoreWeave's overall credit rating is a B+ at S&P Credit Ratings, which is junk bond territory. With rates in general having risen lately, it's natural that highly-leveraged companies, such as CoreWeave, are affected, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. CoreWeave "has capital expenditure levels that are almost hyperscaler-like, but it doesn't have the hyperscaler balance sheet," Nolan said.Tech sector hitCoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares of Oracle closed down nearly 9% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%.The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite closing down 1.9%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest.Another neocloud stock, Nebius, dropped 10%. Dell cratered by roughly 11%.Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to surging supply of new bonds.  For instance, hyperscalers Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle together have issued more than $228 billion in bonds, as of Oct. 13, according to LSEG. That is more than double the amount seen in all of 2025. All but Oracle have investment-grade ratings at S&P Credit Ratings.Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according to JPMorgan. By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said. — CNBC's Seema Mody contributed reporting.

schema.headline: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
